Check the balance of a split or of a set of resamples

Source: R/balance_check.R
balance_check.Rd

balance_check() compares the assessment set of each split with its analysis set. For a three-way split, it compares the validation set and the testing set each with the training set. It reports a standardized mean difference (SMD) for each variable and the energy distance for all variables together. It works with any rset or rsplit, so you can compare balanced folds with ordinary rsample::vfold_cv() folds.

Usage

balance_check(x, ..., max_n = 2000, variance_ratio = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'rset'
balance_check(x, ..., max_n = 2000, variance_ratio = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'rsplit'
balance_check(x, ..., max_n = 2000, variance_ratio = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'three_way_split'
balance_check(x, ..., max_n = 2000, variance_ratio = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'balance_check'
summary(object, ..., threshold = 0.1, by = c("split", "variable"))

Arguments

x

An rset (for example from balanced_vfold_cv()), an rsplit (for example from balanced_initial_split()), or a three-way split (from balanced_initial_validation_split() or rsample::initial_validation_split()).

...

For balance_check(), <tidy-select> columns to check. If empty, the balance and exact columns stored in x are used. For summary(), not used and must be empty.

max_n

The largest number of rows per set for the energy distance. Larger sets are subsampled at random to keep memory use low.

variance_ratio

If TRUE, also report the variance ratio of each numeric variable.

object

A balance_check object.

threshold

The absolute SMD above which summary() counts a variable in n_over. A value within rounding error of threshold (1.5e-8) counts as equal to it, so it isn't counted.

by

"split" for one row per split, or "variable" for one row per variable across the splits.

Value

A tibble with class balance_check. It has the ID columns of x, and the columns variable, level, statistic ("smd", "energy", or "variance_ratio"), and value. Energy rows have NA in variable and level.

summary() with by = "split" returns a tibble with one row per split. It has the ID columns and these columns:

  • max_abs_smd: the largest absolute SMD in the split, with the variable and level it belongs to (the first one if several tie).

  • mean_abs_smd: the mean over the variables of their largest absolute SMD.

  • n_over: the number of variables whose largest absolute SMD is above threshold.

  • n_variables: the number of variables with an SMD that isn't missing.

  • energy: the energy distance.

  • With variance ratios, variance_ratio, the ratio farthest from 1 on the log scale (so 0.25 is farther than 3), and variance_ratio_variable, the variable it belongs to.

If the split has no SMD that isn't missing, max_abs_smd, mean_abs_smd, variable, and level are NA. If it has no energy row, energy is NA.

With by = "variable", it returns one row per variable, with median_abs_smd and max_abs_smd (the median and the largest of the variable's largest absolute SMD in each split), the level and the ID columns of the split with the largest, n_over (the number of splits where it is above threshold), and n_splits (the number of splits where the variable has an SMD that isn't missing). With variance ratios, it also has variance_ratio, the ratio farthest from 1 over the splits.

Each split must have its own ID, so no ID may have more than one energy row. Only the ID columns that balance_check() made are used, so columns you add are ignored. If you rename an ID column, the columns whose names start with id are used instead. If you drop one, splits that differ only in it would merge, so summary() gives an error and printing shows the rows.

Details

For a numeric variable, the SMD is the difference in means (assessment minus analysis) divided by the pooled standard deviation, sqrt((var_assessment + var_analysis) / 2). For a categorical variable, there is one SMD per level, from the proportions of that level. Values under 0.1 in absolute size are often taken as good balance. If both sets have zero variance but different means, the SMD is Inf or -Inf; the plot shows these values at the edge of the panel.

Stored exact columns with whole numbers are treated as categories, as the split functions treat them, so they get one SMD per level and no variance ratio. This holds whether you name them or not. Other whole-number columns are numeric.

With variance_ratio = TRUE, each numeric variable also gets the variance of the assessment set divided by the variance of the analysis set. It is 1 when the spreads are equal, and values between 0.5 and 2 are often taken as good balance. The SMD can be 0 while the spreads differ, and the variance ratio shows which variable differs. A variance within rounding error of zero counts as zero: if both are zero, the ratio is 1, and if one is, it is 0 or Inf. With fewer than two values in a set, it is NA.

Missing values are dropped variable by variable for the SMD and the variance ratio. A variable with missing values also gets an SMD for the share of its values that are missing, with level "(missing)". In summary(), this row counts as one more level of the variable. The energy distance uses all rows. It encodes missing values as the split functions do with na = "include": a numeric variable gets the mean of its observed values plus an indicator of which values are missing, and a categorical variable gets a level for them. So with missing values, it compares the encoded data, not only the observed values.

The energy distance is the V-statistic 2 E|X - Y| - E|X - X'| - E|Y - Y'| on the standardized variables (one indicator column per categorical level). It is 0 when the two sets have the same distribution, and it also detects differences in spread and shape.

Printing the result shows a short table. For one split, it has the SMD of each variable and level. For up to 10 splits, it has one row per split, as from summary(). For more splits, it has one row per variable, as from summary(by = "variable"). Columns that don't fit the width of the console are left out, and a note names them. Printing counts SMDs over 0.1; use summary() with threshold for another value. Use tibble::as_tibble() to see all rows.

summary() first reduces each variable in each split to its largest absolute SMD, over its levels and its "(missing)" row. So a variable with many levels counts once, like a numeric variable. The largest absolute SMD of a split shows the worst variable, but it tends to grow with the number of variables: in random splits of 30 rows against 270, it averaged 0.21 with 2 variables and 0.48 with 40. The mean across variables stayed near 0.15 in such splits, so it is better for comparing splits that check different numbers of variables. The rule of thumb of 0.1 is hard to meet with small sets: in the same random splits, one variable's absolute SMD was under 0.1 only about 40% of the time. An exact column also can't do better than whole rows allow.

Examples

set.seed(1)
folds <- balanced_vfold_cv(
  sim_patients,
  v = 5,
  balance = c(age, income, diagnosis)
)
balance_check(folds)
#> # Balance check: 5 splits, 3 variables
#> # 0 of 5 splits have a variable with |SMD| > 0.1, mean energy distance 0.023
#> 
#> id     max |SMD|  variable         mean |SMD|  over 0.1  energy
#> Fold1    0.00927  diagnosis: mild     0.00318       0/3  0.0218
#> Fold2    0.00927  diagnosis: mild     0.00322       0/3  0.0152
#> Fold3    0.00927  diagnosis: mild     0.00349       0/3  0.0193
#> Fold4    0.00927  diagnosis: mild     0.00326       0/3  0.0243
#> Fold5    0.0373   diagnosis: mild     0.0125        0/3  0.0343
#> 
#> # summary() gives this table as a tibble, and tibble::as_tibble() gives all
#> # 30 rows.
summary(balance_check(folds))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   id    max_abs_smd variable  level mean_abs_smd n_over n_variables energy
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>  <int>       <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Fold1     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00318      0           3 0.0218
#> 2 Fold2     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00322      0           3 0.0152
#> 3 Fold3     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00349      0           3 0.0193
#> 4 Fold4     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00326      0           3 0.0243
#> 5 Fold5     0.0373  diagnosis mild       0.0125       0           3 0.0343
summary(balance_check(folds), by = "variable")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>   variable  median_abs_smd max_abs_smd level id    n_over n_splits
#>   <chr>              <dbl>       <dbl> <chr> <chr>  <int>    <int>
#> 1 age             0.000230    0.000482 NA    Fold3      0        5
#> 2 income          0.000242    0.000735 NA    Fold3      0        5
#> 3 diagnosis       0.00927     0.0373   mild  Fold5      0        5
summary(balance_check(folds, variance_ratio = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 10
#>   id    max_abs_smd variable  level mean_abs_smd n_over n_variables energy
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>  <int>       <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Fold1     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00318      0           3 0.0218
#> 2 Fold2     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00322      0           3 0.0152
#> 3 Fold3     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00349      0           3 0.0193
#> 4 Fold4     0.00927 diagnosis mild       0.00326      0           3 0.0243
#> 5 Fold5     0.0373  diagnosis mild       0.0125       0           3 0.0343
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: variance_ratio <dbl>, variance_ratio_variable <chr>

# Compare with ordinary folds
random_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(sim_patients, v = 5)
summary(balance_check(random_folds, age, income, diagnosis))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   id    max_abs_smd variable  level mean_abs_smd n_over n_variables energy
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>  <int>       <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Fold1       0.280 diagnosis mild         0.173      3           3 0.0857
#> 2 Fold2       0.291 income    NA           0.237      3           3 0.102 
#> 3 Fold3       0.343 diagnosis none         0.190      2           3 0.133 
#> 4 Fold4       0.191 diagnosis mild         0.101      1           3 0.0567
#> 5 Fold5       0.207 diagnosis none         0.128      2           3 0.0671
